label: Prop:FiniteDimHilbert
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{Prop:FiniteDimHilbert}
Let ${\boldsymbol{p}}=(p_n)$ be a basis of ${\mathcal{N}}_{{\boldsymbol{p}}}={\rm span}\{p_n\}_{n=1}^{N_0}\subset {\mathcal{S}}'$. Then, there exists
 a vector of functionals ${\boldsymbol{\phi}}=(\phi_n)$ with $\phi_1,\dots,\phi_{N_0}\in {\mathcal{S}}$ such that
 $\langle p_n, \phi_m\rangle = \delta_{m,n}$ (biorthogonality).
 
The resulting biorthogonal system $({\boldsymbol{p}}, {\boldsymbol{\phi}})$ is called {\em universal} and it allows us to identify the dual pair of 
Hilbert spaces  ${\mathcal{H}}_0=({\mathcal{N}}_{{\boldsymbol{p}}},|\cdot|_{{\mathrm{R}}_{\boldsymbol{\phi}}}) \subset {\mathcal{S}}'$ and
${\mathcal{H}}'_0=({\mathcal{N}}_{{\boldsymbol{\phi}}},|\cdot|_{{\mathrm{R}}_{\boldsymbol{p}}}) \subset {\mathcal{S}}$ equipped with the (semi-)inner
products
\begin{align}
\langle f_1,f_2\rangle_{{\mathrm{R}}_{\boldsymbol{\phi}}} = \sum_{n=1}^{N_0} \langle \phi_n,f_1 \rangle\langle \phi_n,f_2 \rangle\\ 
\langle \varphi_1,\varphi_2\rangle_{{\mathrm{R}}_{\boldsymbol{p}}} = \sum_{n=1}^{N_0} \langle p_n,\varphi_1 \rangle \langle p_n,\varphi_2 \rangle,
\end{align}
which are well-defined for any $f_1,f_2 \in {\mathcal{S}}'$ and $\varphi_1,\varphi_2 \in {\mathcal{S}}$.
The same construction applies with any dual pair $({\mathcal{H}},{\mathcal{H}}')$ of Hilbert spaces such that
${\mathcal{S}} \overset{}{\hookrightarrow} {\mathcal{H}} \overset{}{\hookrightarrow} {\mathcal{S}}'$ in place of $({\mathcal{S}},{\mathcal{S}}')$, which enables the use of
{\em non-universal} biorthogonal systems.

title: Proof
body_md:
Let us assume first that ${\boldsymbol{\phi}} \subset {\mathcal{S}}$, so that the augmented pair \eqref{Eq:Aplus} of
Part I is available. Items 1--3, 6, and 7 are then transcriptions of the results of Part I,
while Items 4 and 5 are new.

\medskip
\emph{Inner product and embeddings (Items 1 and 3)}:
The augmented operator ${\mathrm{B}}_+={\mathrm{B}}+{\mathrm{R}}_{{\boldsymbol{\phi}}}$ is positive-definite on ${\mathcal{S}}$ with
$|f|^2_{{\mathrm{B}}_+}=\|{\mathrm{L}} f\|^2_{L_2}+|{\boldsymbol{\phi}}(f)|_2^2$, and $({\mathrm{A}}_+,{\mathrm{B}}_+)$ is a compatible
Riesz pair (Part I, Theorem~\ref{I-Thm:Augmentation}). Theorem~\ref{I-Theo:HilbertPositiveDef} of
Part I then identifies ${\mathcal{H}}_{\mathrm{L}}=\overline{({\mathcal{S}},|\cdot|_{{\mathrm{B}}_+})}$ as a
Hilbert--Gelfand space, which yields the embeddings ${\mathcal{S}} \overset{d}{\hookrightarrow} {\mathcal{H}}_{\mathrm{L}} \overset{d}{\hookrightarrow} {\mathcal{S}}'$
and the completion formula of Item 3. The polarization of $|\cdot|_{{\mathrm{B}}_+}$ gives the inner
product, where the factorization ${\mathrm{B}}={\mathrm{L}}^\ast{\mathrm{L}}$ turns $\langle {\mathrm{B}} f, g\rangle$ into
$\langle {\mathrm{L}} f, {\mathrm{L}} g\rangle_{L_2}$; this is \eqref{Eq:InnerProd}.

\medskip
\emph{Direct-sum decomposition (Item 2)}:
The orthogonal decomposition ${\mathcal{H}}_{\mathrm{L}}={\mathcal{H}}'={\mathcal{H}}'_{{\mathrm{A}}}\oplus {\mathcal{N}}_{{\boldsymbol{p}}}$ is Item 3
of Theorem~\ref{I-Thm:Augmentation} of Part I. Its infinite-dimensional component is
characterized by the boundary condition ${\boldsymbol{\phi}}(f)={\boldsymbol{0}}$, because
${\mathcal{H}}'_{{\mathrm{A}}}\subset {\mathcal{S}}'_{{\boldsymbol{\phi}}}$, and it coincides with ${\mathrm{L}}^{-1}_{{\boldsymbol{\phi}}}(L_2)$
because ${\mathrm{L}}^{-1}_{{\boldsymbol{\phi}}}$ maps $L_2$ isometrically onto ${\mathcal{H}}'_{{\mathrm{A}}}$ (Part I,
Proposition~\ref{I-Prop:Factorization}, Item 1). This gives
${\mathcal{H}}_{{\mathrm{L}}, {\boldsymbol{\phi}}}={\mathcal{H}}'_{{\mathrm{A}}}$ with $\|f\|_{{\mathcal{H}}_{{\mathrm{L}}, {\boldsymbol{\phi}}}}=\|{\mathrm{L}} f\|_{L_2}$.
The finite-dimensional component is the effective null space of ${\mathrm{L}}$, since the continuous
extension of ${\mathrm{L}}$ annihilates ${\mathcal{N}}_{{\mathrm{B}}}={\mathcal{N}}_{{\boldsymbol{p}}}$, and nothing else in
${\mathcal{H}}_{\mathrm{L}}$.

\medskip
\emph{Riesz maps (Item 6)}:
Item 4 of Theorem~\ref{I-Thm:Augmentation} of Part I states that
${\mathrm{A}}_+={\mathrm{A}}_{{\boldsymbol{\phi}}}+{\mathrm{R}}_{{\boldsymbol{p}}}$ and ${\mathrm{B}}_+={\mathrm{L}}^\ast{\mathrm{L}}+{\mathrm{R}}_{{\boldsymbol{\phi}}}$ are isometric
and mutually inverse, which identifies them as the Riesz maps ${\mathrm{J}}_{{\mathcal{H}}'_{\mathrm{L}}}$ and
${\mathrm{J}}_{{\mathcal{H}}_{\mathrm{L}}}$. Since the duality pairing is block-diagonal with respect to the two direct
sums of \eqref{Eq:AugmentedPair}, the restriction of ${\mathrm{A}}_+$ to ${\mathcal{H}}_{{\mathrm{A}}}$ is
${\mathrm{A}}_{{\boldsymbol{\phi}}}: {\mathcal{H}}_{{\mathrm{A}}}\to {\mathcal{H}}'_{{\mathrm{A}}}={\mathcal{H}}_{{\mathrm{L}},{\boldsymbol{\phi}}}$, which is the Riesz map
of ${\mathcal{H}}_{{\mathrm{A}}}$. Its factorization ${\mathrm{A}}_{{\boldsymbol{\phi}}}={\mathrm{L}}^{-1}_{{\boldsymbol{\phi}}}{\mathrm{L}}^{-1\ast}_{{\boldsymbol{\phi}}}$
is \eqref{Eq:Factorization}.

\medskip
\emph{Homogeneous part (Item 7)}:
The first equality is the definition \eqref{Eq:HB} of the homogeneous space, since
$|\varphi|_{{\mathrm{B}}}=\|{\mathrm{L}} \varphi\|_{L_2}$ on ${\mathcal{S}}$. Item 1 of
Theorem~\ref{I-Thm:Concretization} of Part I identifies ${\mathrm{P}}^\ast_{{\boldsymbol{\phi}}}$ as an isometric
isomorphism $\dot{{\mathcal{H}}}_{{\mathrm{B}}}\to{\mathcal{H}}'_{{\mathrm{A}}}={\mathcal{H}}_{{\mathrm{L}},{\boldsymbol{\phi}}}$. Moreover, since the
direct sum of Item 2 is orthogonal, the quotient norm on ${\mathcal{H}}_{\mathrm{L}}/{\mathcal{N}}_{{\boldsymbol{p}}}$ is attained
at $f_0={\mathrm{P}}^\ast_{{\boldsymbol{\phi}}}f$ with
$\min_{p\in{\mathcal{N}}_{{\boldsymbol{p}}}}\|f+p\|_{{\mathcal{H}}_{\mathrm{L}}}=\|f_0\|_{{\mathcal{H}}_{\mathrm{L}}}=\|{\mathrm{L}} f\|_{L_2}$, which
yields the isometry ${\mathcal{H}}_{\mathrm{L}}/{\mathcal{N}}_{{\boldsymbol{p}}}\cong{\mathcal{H}}_{{\mathrm{L}},{\boldsymbol{\phi}}}\cong\dot{{\mathcal{H}}}_{{\mathrm{B}}}$.
The duality with ${\mathcal{H}}_{{\mathrm{A}}}$ and the identification of the Riesz map $\pi{\mathrm{A}}$ constitute
Clause (ii) of Definition~\ref{Def:Intrinsic}, while the identity $\pi{\mathrm{A}}_{{\boldsymbol{\phi}}}=\pi{\mathrm{A}}$
and the independence of $\dot{{\mathcal{H}}}_{{\mathrm{B}}}$, ${\mathcal{H}}_{{\mathrm{A}}}$, and $\pi{\mathrm{A}}$ from the choice
of ${\boldsymbol{\phi}}$ are Items 2 and 3 of Theorem~\ref{I-Thm:Concretization}.

\medskip
\emph{Equivalence of norms (Item 4)}:
As an alternative to $({\boldsymbol{\phi}},{\boldsymbol{p}})$, we consider another biorthogonal 
system $(\widetilde{{\boldsymbol{\phi}}},\widetilde{{\boldsymbol{p}}})$ with $\widetilde{{\boldsymbol{p}}}=(\tilde p_n)$ some basis of ${\mathcal{N}}_{{\boldsymbol{p}}}$,
$\widetilde{{\boldsymbol{\phi}}}=(\widetilde \phi_n)$ with $\widetilde \phi_1, \dots, \widetilde \phi_{N_0} \in {\mathcal{H}}'_{\mathrm{L}}$ and $\langle \widetilde \phi_m, \widetilde p_n\rangle=\delta_{m,n}$ (biorthogonality). The corresponding inner product
induces the Hilbertian norm
\begin{align}
\|f\|_{\widetilde{{\mathcal{H}}}_{\mathrm{L}}}=\left(\|{\mathrm{L}} f\|_{L_2}^2 + \sum_{n=1}^{N_0} |\langle \widetilde{\phi}_n, f \rangle|^2\right)^{\tfrac{1}{2}}.
\end{align}

Since two norms that are equivalent on ${\mathcal{S}}$ yield the same completion, it suffices to
establish the two-sided bound \eqref{Eq:NormEquiv} below.

The upper bound follows from the duality bound \eqref{Eq:DualityBound}, which is
applicable because $\widetilde{\phi}_n \in {\mathcal{H}}'_{\mathrm{L}}$. Together with
$\|{\mathrm{L}} f\|_{L_2}\le \|f\|_{{\mathcal{H}}_{\mathrm{L}}}$, it gives
\begin{align*}
\|f\|^2_{\widetilde{{\mathcal{H}}}_{\mathrm{L}}}\le \|{\mathrm{L}} f\|_{L_2}^2 + \sum_{n=1}^{N_0} \|\widetilde{\phi}_n\|^2_{{\mathcal{H}}'_{\mathrm{L}}}\|f\|^2_{{\mathcal{H}}_{\mathrm{L}}}\le \left(1 + \sum_{n=1}^{N_0} \|\widetilde{\phi}_n\|^2_{{\mathcal{H}}'_{\mathrm{L}}}\right) \|f\|^2_{{\mathcal{H}}_{\mathrm{L}}}.
\end{align*}
The lower bound cannot be obtained by exchanging the roles of the two systems, for the dual norm
$\|\cdot\|_{\widetilde{{\mathcal{H}}}'_{\mathrm{L}}}$ is not available before the equivalence has been
established. We rely instead on the structure of ${\mathrm{L}}$. By Items 1 and 2, the operator
${\mathrm{L}}: {\mathcal{H}}_{\mathrm{L}} \to L_2$ is bounded and surjective with $\ker {\mathrm{L}}={\mathcal{N}}_{{\boldsymbol{p}}}$, so that the
induced map ${\mathcal{H}}_{\mathrm{L}}/{\mathcal{N}}_{{\boldsymbol{p}}}\to L_2$ is a continuous bijection between Banach spaces.
Its inverse is continuous as well, which provides a constant $c_{\mathrm{L}}$ such that
\begin{align}
\label{Eq:BoundedBelow}
\min_{p \in {\mathcal{N}}_{{\boldsymbol{p}}}}\|f+p\|_{{\mathcal{H}}_{\mathrm{L}}}\le c_{\mathrm{L}} \|{\mathrm{L}} f\|_{L_2},\qquad f \in {\mathcal{H}}_{\mathrm{L}}.
\end{align}
The subspace ${\mathcal{H}}_{{\mathrm{L}},\widetilde{{\boldsymbol{\phi}}}}=\{f \in {\mathcal{H}}_{\mathrm{L}}: \widetilde{{\boldsymbol{\phi}}}(f)={\boldsymbol{0}}\}$ is
closed, because the $\widetilde{\phi}_n$ are continuous on ${\mathcal{H}}_{\mathrm{L}}$, and biorthogonality makes
it a topological complement of ${\mathcal{N}}_{{\boldsymbol{p}}}$. On such a complement, the minimum in
\eqref{Eq:BoundedBelow} is equivalent to the norm itself, which yields a constant $c'_{\mathrm{L}}$ with
$\|f_0\|_{{\mathcal{H}}_{\mathrm{L}}}\le c'_{\mathrm{L}}\|{\mathrm{L}} f_0\|_{L_2}$ for every $f_0 \in {\mathcal{H}}_{{\mathrm{L}},\widetilde{{\boldsymbol{\phi}}}}$.
We now split $f=f_0+\tilde p$ with
$\tilde p={\mathrm{R}}_{\widetilde{{\boldsymbol{p}}}}{\mathrm{R}}_{\widetilde{{\boldsymbol{\phi}}}}f=\sum_{n=1}^{N_0} \tilde p_n \langle \widetilde{\phi}_n, f\rangle \in {\mathcal{N}}_{{\boldsymbol{p}}}$
and $f_0=f-\tilde p\in {\mathcal{H}}_{{\mathrm{L}},\widetilde{{\boldsymbol{\phi}}}}$. Since ${\mathrm{L}} f_0={\mathrm{L}} f$, the
triangle and Cauchy--Schwarz inequalities give
\begin{align*}
\|f\|_{{\mathcal{H}}_{\mathrm{L}}}\le \|f_0\|_{{\mathcal{H}}_{\mathrm{L}}} + \|\tilde p\|_{{\mathcal{H}}_{\mathrm{L}}}
\le c'_{\mathrm{L}} \|{\mathrm{L}} f\|_{L_2} + C_{\widetilde{{\boldsymbol{p}}}}\,|\widetilde{{\boldsymbol{\phi}}}(f)|_2
\le \sqrt{{c'_{\mathrm{L}}}^2+C_{\widetilde{{\boldsymbol{p}}}}^2}\;\|f\|_{\widetilde{{\mathcal{H}}}_{\mathrm{L}}}
\end{align*}
with $C_{\widetilde{{\boldsymbol{p}}}}=\big(\sum_{n=1}^{N_0}\|\tilde p_n\|^2_{{\mathcal{H}}_{\mathrm{L}}}\big)^{\tfrac12}$. The
two bounds combine into
\begin{align}
\forall f \in {\mathcal{H}}_{\mathrm{L}}:\quad A_1 \|f\|_{{\mathcal{H}}_{\mathrm{L}}} \le \|f\|_{\widetilde{{\mathcal{H}}}_{\mathrm{L}}} \le A_2 \|f\|_{{\mathcal{H}}_{\mathrm{L}}} 
\label{Eq:NormEquiv}
\end{align}
with $A_1=\big({c'_{\mathrm{L}}}^2+C_{\widetilde{{\boldsymbol{p}}}}^2\big)^{-\tfrac{1}{2}}$ and
$A_2=\left(1 + \sum_{n=1}^{N_0} \|\widetilde{\phi}_n\|^2_{{\mathcal{H}}'_{\mathrm{L}}}\right)^{\tfrac{1}{2}}$.

\medskip
\emph{Explicit representation (Item 5)}:
Let $f \in {\mathcal{H}}_{\mathrm{L}}$ and let us set $w={\mathrm{L}} f \in L_2$,
$p=(\mathrm{Id}-{\mathrm{P}}^\ast_{{\boldsymbol{\phi}}})f={\mathrm{R}}_{{\boldsymbol{p}}}{\mathrm{R}}_{{\boldsymbol{\phi}}}f \in {\mathcal{N}}_{{\boldsymbol{p}}}$ and
$f_0={\mathrm{P}}^\ast_{{\boldsymbol{\phi}}}f \in {\mathcal{H}}_{{\mathrm{L}},{\boldsymbol{\phi}}}$, which is the decomposition of Item 2. The
inversion relation ${\mathrm{L}}^{-1}_{{\boldsymbol{\phi}}}{\mathrm{L}}={\mathrm{P}}^\ast_{{\boldsymbol{\phi}}}$ of Part I
(Proposition~\ref{I-Prop:Factorization}, Item 1) then gives $f_0={\mathrm{L}}^{-1}_{{\boldsymbol{\phi}}}\{w\}$.
Likewise, $f^\ast={\mathrm{B}} f={\mathrm{L}}^\ast w \in {\mathrm{L}}^\ast(L_2)={\mathcal{H}}'_{{\mathrm{L}},{\boldsymbol{\phi}}}$, so that the
definition ${\mathrm{L}}^{-1}_{{\boldsymbol{\phi}}}={\mathrm{A}}_{{\boldsymbol{\phi}}}{\mathrm{L}}^\ast$ in \eqref{Eq:gInverse} yields
${\mathrm{A}}_{{\boldsymbol{\phi}}}\{f^\ast\}={\mathrm{A}}_{{\boldsymbol{\phi}}}{\mathrm{L}}^\ast w={\mathrm{L}}^{-1}_{{\boldsymbol{\phi}}}\{w\}=f_0$. This
proves the two forms of \eqref{Eq:Sumdecomp1}. The triplet $(w,f^\ast,p)$ is unique
because the sum in Item 2 is direct, while ${\mathrm{L}}$ and ${\mathrm{L}}^\ast$ are injective on
${\mathcal{H}}_{{\mathrm{L}},{\boldsymbol{\phi}}}$ and $L_2$, respectively.

\medskip
\emph{Non-universal systems}:
Let us finally consider a system $(\widetilde{{\boldsymbol{p}}},\widetilde{{\boldsymbol{\phi}}})$ with
$\widetilde{{\boldsymbol{\phi}}}\subset {\mathcal{H}}'_{\mathrm{L}}$. The set ${\mathcal{H}}_{\mathrm{L}}$ and its topology are the ones
that have just been constructed from a universal system, while Item 4 shows that the norm
induced by $\widetilde{{\boldsymbol{\phi}}}$ is equivalent to $\|\cdot\|_{{\mathcal{H}}_{\mathrm{L}}}$. All the statements
are therefore preserved, the splitting of Item 2 being the only ingredient that depends on the
choice of the system: the component
$\tilde p={\mathrm{R}}_{\widetilde{{\boldsymbol{p}}}}{\mathrm{R}}_{\widetilde{{\boldsymbol{\phi}}}}\{f\}$ differs from
$p={\mathrm{R}}_{{\boldsymbol{p}}}{\mathrm{R}}_{{\boldsymbol{\phi}}}\{f\}$, while $w={\mathrm{L}} f$ is common to all splittings.

title: Proof
body_md:
Let us fix a universal biorthogonal system $({\boldsymbol{\phi}},{\boldsymbol{p}})$, so that
${\mathcal{H}}'_{\mathrm{L}}={\mathcal{H}}_{{\mathrm{A}}}\oplus {\mathcal{N}}_{{\boldsymbol{\phi}}}$ with ${\mathcal{N}}_{{\boldsymbol{\phi}}}\subset {\mathcal{S}}$, and
let us recall that ${\mathcal{H}}_{{\mathrm{A}}}=\{\nu \in {\mathcal{H}}'_{\mathrm{L}}: {\boldsymbol{p}}(\nu)={\boldsymbol{0}}\}$, which is the second
equivalence in \eqref{Eq:Afprop}.

\medskip
\emph{Sufficiency}:
Let $\nu \in {\mathcal{H}}_{{\mathrm{A}}}$. Since ${\mathrm{P}}_{{\boldsymbol{\phi}}}$ acts as the identity on ${\mathcal{H}}_{{\mathrm{A}}}$, we
have that ${\mathrm{A}}_{{\boldsymbol{\phi}}}\{\nu\}={\mathrm{A}}\{\nu\}-{\mathrm{R}}_{{\boldsymbol{p}}}{\mathrm{R}}_{{\boldsymbol{\phi}}}{\mathrm{A}}\{\nu\}$. The first
term of the right-hand side is in ${\mathcal{H}}_{{\mathrm{L}},{\boldsymbol{\phi}}}$ by Item \ref{Item:ExplicitRep} of
Theorem \ref{Theo:NativeSpace}, while the second one is in ${\mathcal{N}}_{{\boldsymbol{p}}}$, which yields
${\mathrm{A}}\{\nu\} \in {\mathcal{H}}_{{\mathrm{L}},{\boldsymbol{\phi}}}\oplus {\mathcal{N}}_{{\boldsymbol{p}}}={\mathcal{H}}_{\mathrm{L}}$.

\medskip
\emph{Necessity}:
Let $\phi \in {\mathcal{N}}_{{\boldsymbol{\phi}}}\backslash\{0\}$ and let us assume that
${\mathrm{A}}\{\phi\} \in {\mathcal{H}}_{\mathrm{L}}$. The consistency requirement \eqref{Eq:Consistency} gives
$\phi=({\mathrm{L}}^\ast{\mathrm{L}})\{{\mathrm{A}}\phi\}$, while Item \ref{Item:ExplicitRep} of
Theorem \ref{Theo:NativeSpace} places the right-hand side in ${\mathcal{H}}_{{\mathrm{A}}}$. Hence
$\phi \in {\mathcal{H}}_{{\mathrm{A}}}\cap {\mathcal{N}}_{{\boldsymbol{\phi}}}=\{0\}$, which is a contradiction. A general
$\nu \in {\mathcal{H}}'_{\mathrm{L}}$ splits as $\nu=\psi+\phi$ with $\psi \in {\mathcal{H}}_{{\mathrm{A}}}$ and
$\phi \in {\mathcal{N}}_{{\boldsymbol{\phi}}}$; since ${\mathrm{A}}\{\psi\} \in {\mathcal{H}}_{\mathrm{L}}$ by the previous step, the
hypothesis ${\mathrm{A}}\{\nu\} \in {\mathcal{H}}_{\mathrm{L}}$ forces ${\mathrm{A}}\{\phi\} \in {\mathcal{H}}_{\mathrm{L}}$, and hence
$\phi=0$.

\medskip
\emph{Decomposition}:
Item \ref{Item:ExplicitRep} of Theorem \ref{Theo:NativeSpace} gives
$f={\mathrm{A}}_{{\boldsymbol{\phi}}}\{f^\ast\}+q$ with $q \in {\mathcal{N}}_{{\boldsymbol{p}}}$ and $f^\ast=({\mathrm{L}}^\ast{\mathrm{L}})\{f\}$, while the first step
gives ${\mathrm{A}}_{{\boldsymbol{\phi}}}\{f^\ast\}={\mathrm{A}}\{f^\ast\}-p'$ with $p' \in {\mathcal{N}}_{{\boldsymbol{p}}}$. This is
\eqref{Eq:DecomposeAgostic} with $p=q-p'$. As for uniqueness, let us suppose that
${\mathrm{A}}\{f^\ast_1\}+p_1={\mathrm{A}}\{f^\ast_2\}+p_2$ with $f^\ast_1,f^\ast_2 \in {\mathcal{H}}_{{\mathrm{A}}}$. Then,
${\mathrm{A}}\{f^\ast_1-f^\ast_2\} \in {\mathcal{N}}_{{\boldsymbol{p}}}$, and the application of $({\mathrm{L}}^\ast{\mathrm{L}})$ gives
$f^\ast_1=f^\ast_2$.

label: Rem:Consistency
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{Rem:Consistency}
The consistency requirement \eqref{Eq:Consistency} is automatically met for
$\varphi \in {\mathcal{S}}_{{\boldsymbol{p}}}$ (Part I, Theorem~\ref{I-Thm:Concretization}, Item 2), and it holds
for any conditional inverse of Green's type. In particular, when ${\mathrm{L}}$ is shift-invariant, the
canonical Fourier-domain inverse of Section \ref{Sec:RKHS} satisfies the stronger algebraic
identity $({\mathrm{L}}^\ast{\mathrm{L}}){\mathrm{A}}=\mathrm{Id}$ on ${\mathcal{S}}$, which implies \eqref{Eq:Consistency}.

label: Rem:TwoReadings
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{Rem:TwoReadings}
Let us contrast two ways of expressing that ${\mathrm{A}}$ inverts ${\mathrm{B}}={\mathrm{L}}^\ast{\mathrm{L}}$. The first is
${\mathrm{B}}{\mathrm{A}}=\mathrm{Id}$ on ${\mathcal{S}}_{{\boldsymbol{p}}}$, understood through the canonical Hilbertian extension
${\mathrm{B}}: {\mathcal{H}}_{\mathrm{L}} \to {\mathcal{H}}_{{\mathrm{A}}}$; this statement is well-formed for every conditional
inverse, and it holds for all of them. The second is the Green's-function version
${\mathrm{B}}{\mathrm{A}}\{\varphi\}=\varphi$ for all $\varphi \in {\mathcal{S}}$, which requires an interpretation
of ${\mathrm{B}}$ on the range ${\mathrm{A}}({\mathcal{S}})\not\subset {\mathcal{H}}_{\mathrm{L}}$. The canonical interpretation is
the extension by transposition: since ${\mathrm{B}}$ is symmetric, we set
$\langle \widetilde{{\mathrm{B}}} u, \psi\rangle := \langle u, {\mathrm{B}}\psi\rangle$ for every
$u \in {\mathcal{S}}'$ such that the right-hand side is well-defined for all $\psi \in {\mathcal{S}}$. This
extension involves no arbitrary choice and agrees with the Hilbertian one on ${\mathcal{H}}_{\mathrm{L}}$,
since both satisfy $\langle \widetilde{{\mathrm{B}}} f,\psi\rangle=\langle {\mathrm{L}} f, {\mathrm{L}} \psi
\rangle_{L_2}$. The verification that ${\mathrm{A}}({\mathcal{S}})$ lies in the domain of $\widetilde{{\mathrm{B}}}$
is immediate for differential operators and follows from degree counting for fractional ones.
Specifically, the conditional inverse for ${\mathrm{L}}=(-\Delta)^{\gamma/2}$ is ${\mathrm{A}}=(-\Delta)^{-\gamma}$, the fractional integrator or Riesz potential of order $2\gamma$.
For $\varphi \in {\mathcal{S}}( \mathbb{R}^d)$, $(-\Delta)^{-\gamma}\{\varphi\}$ with $2\gamma \notin 2 \mathbb{N}$ exhibits a growth
$|{\boldsymbol{x}}|^{2\gamma-d}$---with a logarithmic correction when $2\gamma-d$ is
an even integer---that is offset by the algebraic decay $|{\boldsymbol{x}}|^{-(d+2\gamma)}$ of ${\mathrm{B}}\{\psi\}$
induced by the singularity of the symbol at ${\boldsymbol{\omega}}={\boldsymbol{0}}$; the product decays like
$|{\boldsymbol{x}}|^{-2d}$, which is integrable at infinity irrespective of $\gamma$. Under this reading,
the second version is a strictly stronger requirement than the first: it selects the
Green's-type conditional inverses, and it pins down ${\mathrm{A}}$ on ${\mathcal{N}}_{{\boldsymbol{\phi}}}$ up to
${\mathcal{N}}_{{\mathrm{L}}^\ast{\mathrm{L}}}$-components.

title: Proof
body_md:
Every $\nu_m \in {\mathcal{H}}'$ has a unique Riesz representer
$\nu_m^\ast={\mathrm{J}}_{{\mathcal{H}}'}\{\nu_m\} \in {\mathcal{H}}$, which satisfies
$\langle \nu_{m'}, \nu^\ast_m\rangle=\langle \nu_{m'}^\ast,\nu_m^\ast \rangle_{{\mathcal{H}}}
=\langle \nu_{m'},\nu_m \rangle_{{\mathcal{H}}'}=[{\bf{G}}]_{m',m}$, where ${\bf{G}} \in  \mathbb{R}^{M \times M}$ is
the {\em Gram matrix} of the system. The assumption of linear independence ensures that ${\bf{G}}$
is positive-definite and hence invertible.

\medskip
\emph{Lagrangian and duality}:
By introducing the multipliers ${\boldsymbol{\lambda}}=(\lambda_m) \in  \mathbb{R}^M$, we write the Lagrangian of
\eqref{Eq:Ginterpol} as
\begin{align*}
\mathcal L(f,{\boldsymbol{\lambda}})
&= \frac12 \|f\|_{{\mathcal{H}}}^2
+ \sum_{m=1}^M \lambda_m \big( z_m - \langle \nu_m , f \rangle \big)\\
&= \frac12
   \Big\| f - \sum_{m=1}^M \lambda_m \nu_m^\ast \Big\|_{{\mathcal{H}}}^2
   - \frac12
   \Big\| \sum_{m=1}^M \lambda_m \nu_m^\ast \Big\|_{{\mathcal{H}}}^2
   + {\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^\mathsf{T} {\bf{z}},
\end{align*}
where we have used the defining property
$\langle \nu_m, f\rangle=\langle \nu^\ast_m, f\rangle_{{\mathcal{H}}}$ of the Riesz representers and
completed the square. The infimum over $f \in {\mathcal{H}}$ is attained at
$f=\sum_{m=1}^M \lambda_m \nu_m^\ast$, which identifies the dual function as
\begin{align*}
\inf_{f\in{\mathcal{H}}} \mathcal L(f,{\boldsymbol{\lambda}})
= {\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^\mathsf{T} {\bf{z}}
  - \frac12
    \Big\| \sum_{m=1}^M \lambda_m \nu_m \Big\|_{{\mathcal{H}}'}^2
={\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^\mathsf{T} {\bf{z}}-\tfrac{1}{2}{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^\mathsf{T} {\bf{G}} {\boldsymbol{\lambda}} .
\end{align*}
This is the criterion of \eqref{Eq:DualProb}, which proves the claim of duality. The quadratic
form is strictly concave, and its (unique) maximum is achieved for ${\bf{a}}={\bf{G}}^{-1} {\bf{z}}$.

\medskip
\emph{Resolution of the primal problem \eqref{Eq:Ginterpol}}:
Let $g_{\bf{a}}=\sum_{m=1}^M a_m \nu_m^\ast$ with ${\bf{a}}={\bf{G}}^{-1} {\bf{z}}$. Since
$\langle \nu_{m'},g_{\bf{a}}\rangle=\sum_{m=1}^M a_m [{\bf{G}}]_{m',m}=z_{m'}$ for all $m'$, the
feasibility set ${\mathcal{A}}_{\boldsymbol{z}} := \{ f \in {\mathcal{H}} : {\boldsymbol{\nu}}(f)={\bf{z}} \}$ is non-empty. It is
the affine set ${\mathcal{A}}_{\boldsymbol{z}}=g_{\bf{a}} + {\mathcal{H}}_0^\perp$, where
${\mathcal{H}}_0={\rm span}\{\nu^\ast_m\}_{m=1}^M$ and
${\mathcal{H}}_0^\perp=\{f\in {\mathcal{H}}: \langle \nu_m, f\rangle=0,\ m=1,\dots,M\}$. Any feasible
$f=g_{\bf{a}}+h$ with $h \in {\mathcal{H}}_0^\perp$ then satisfies the Pythagorean relation
\begin{align*}
\|f\|^2_{{\mathcal{H}}}= \|g_{\bf{a}}\|^2_{{\mathcal{H}}} + \|f-g_{\bf{a}}\|^2_{{\mathcal{H}}},
\end{align*}
which proves that $f_0=g_{\bf{a}}$ is the unique minimum-norm solution, with
$\|f_0\|^2_{{\mathcal{H}}}={\bf{a}}^\mathsf{T} {\bf{G}} {\bf{a}}={\bf{z}}^\mathsf{T} {\bf{G}}^{-1} {\bf{z}}$.
